extracted.intended_audience: inventors and patent practitioners (attorneys, agents, first-time filers)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance and legal rules for drafting patent claims in a utility nonprovisional application, including claim structure, formalities, drafting do's and don'ts, and strategic considerations (scope vs cost).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-claim questions (understand the invention)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior to writing claim(s) answer these questions: What is the invention? What are the elements that make up the invention? How do the elements relate to one another? Do you have more than one invention? Tangible: Apparatus, machine, composition. Method: Making or Using. Are there multiple embodiments of the same invention?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these questions to identify components, relationships, statutory class (product vs method), and multiple embodiments before drafting claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal requirement: at least one claim particularly pointing out and distinctly defining the invention
rubrics_metrics.description: A nonprovisional patent application must have at least one claim particularly pointing out and distinctly defining the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure claims meet this statutory requirement; claims are the legal definition of what is enforced. Claims must conform to the rest of the specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent vs dependent claim forms
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim may be written in independent or dependent form. An independent claim is a standalone claim that contains all the limitations necessary to define an invention. A dependent claim must refer to a claim previously set forth and must further limit that claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dependent claims incorporate by reference all limitations of the claim to which they refer; dependent claims must add a further limitation (do not remove or replace elements of the parent claim).

rubrics_metrics.name: Support and enablement (written description/enablement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims must be fully supported and enabled by the disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use consistent terminology between specification and claims; ensure claim terms find clear support or antecedent basis in the description so terms are clearly understood by reference to the description (refer to 35 U.S.C. §112 requirements).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims must be a single sentence and ordered by scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims must be drafted as a single sentence. Claims should be arranged in order of scope so the first claim presented is the broadest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Format each claim as one sentence (capital letter to start, period at end); place broadest independent claims first to reflect scope ordering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of claims by statutory category
rubrics_metrics.description: Product - A claim that is directed to elements that can be: Active (a Device/Apparatus), Non-active (Composition or Article of Manufacture), Combination thereof. Method (Process) - A claim that describes/defines a series of acts or steps for performing a desired function or accomplishing an intended result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose appropriate claim category for the invention; do not mix multiple statutory classes in a single claim (e.g., 'A widget and method for using same...').

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent claim structure: preamble, transition, claim body
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim has three parts: 1. Preamble: provides context for the claimed invention (may or may not limit). 2. Transitional phrase: establishes whether the claim is 'open', 'closed' or 'partially open'. 3. Claim body: recites the limitations (structure and/or acts in clear, full, concise terms) necessary to define the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft each part carefully: use the preamble for context (avoid unnecessary functional language), choose the transition to control scope, and recite clear limitations in the body.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preamble guidance (Three Basic Rules #1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every claim needs a preamble, which is the introductory phrase in a claim. The general rule is that the preamble of a claim does not limit the scope of the claim, but try and stay away from functional language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer simple nouns ('A shovel...') rather than functional preambles ('A shovel for digging...') unless the preamble is intended to limit claim scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transitional phrases and meanings (Three Basic Rules #2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Common transitions: 'comprising', 'consisting essentially of', and 'consisting of.' 'Comprising' means the invention includes but is not limited to the elements identified in the claim. 'Consisting essentially of' limits scope to the specified materials or steps 'and those that do not materially affect the basic and novel characteristic(s)'. 'Consisting of' is closed and limits to the elements identified in the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'comprising' most commonly for open scope; avoid non-standard transitional phrases (MPEP 2111.03) which may raise interpretation issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Antecedent basis rule (Three Basic Rules #3)
rubrics_metrics.description: The first time you introduce a limitation you MUST introduce it with either 'a' or 'an' (primary antecedent basis). Subsequently refer to it by 'said' or 'the' (secondary antecedent basis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure every term referenced later in the claims has an earlier antecedent; failure causes ambiguity (e.g., referring to 'said lever' without earlier recitation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Antecedent basis clarity issues (examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: A lack of clarity arises where a claim refers to 'said lever' or 'the lever' when the claim contains no earlier recitation of a lever, or when two different levers are recited earlier and it's unclear which is intended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid ambiguous cross-references; disambiguate by naming or numbering elements or by clear antecedent language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim formalities (formatting and numbering rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: Starts on a separate sheet with the Heading 'Claim Listing'. 1.5 or double spaced. Each claim is a single sentence (begins with a capital letter and ends with a period). 3 independent claims; 20 claims total before excess fees are due. Numbered consecutively in ascending order; original numbering preserved throughout prosecution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe formatting and counting rules to avoid procedural errors and unexpected fees; maintain original numbering during prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to build claim sets (wrapping it all together)
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce components and characterizations necessary for the invention to work and for it to be different than the prior art. Example pattern: 1. A - insert title - comprising: A, B and C. Then dependent claims adding D, E, and specific characterizations using 'further comprising' and 'wherein.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When adding a component use 'further comprising' and explain the connection; when further characterizing something already introduced use 'wherein'. Ensure dependent claims further limit the parent claim (35 U.S.C. 112(d), MPEP 608.01(n)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Drafting approach: focus on the inventive concept
rubrics_metrics.description: Focus on the inventive concept: What features set the invention apart from prior inventions? Identify fundamental elements. Omit unnecessary elements unless they are needed to distinguish over prior inventions. Select broad terms and identify their relationship carefully. Claim review and revision: Remove unnecessary claim elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for claims that capture the core inventive features broadly while excluding unnecessary detail; balance breadth with patentability over prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability summary: novelty, non-obviousness, utility
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed invention must be novel, non-obvious and have a utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims alone do not make an invention patentable — ensure invention meets statutory requirements and the specification supports claims; don't treat the patent as a marketing brochure; analyze advantages and multiple inventive features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify fundamental elements and prior art awareness
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand the disclosure of the prior inventions. What have competitors previously done? Conduct a patentability search. Define the potential claim elements. Consider alternative embodiments; prior disclosures may help develop alternatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use prior art search results to shape claim scope and identify novel elements; draft claims to cover key embodiments and reasonable alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Costs versus coverage tradeoff
rubrics_metrics.description: How much can you afford to spend on claims? Independent in excess of 3 = $105 per (micro entity). Total claims in excess of 20 = $20 per (micro entity). Claim fees for small entity are double micro entity. Not just at time of filing, but during prosecution. Consider desired patent scope end state: broadest possible valid claim (longer prosecution) vs claims with a range of claim scopes (higher claim costs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan claim quantity and scope according to budget and enforcement goals; factor in future prosecution costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim review: avoid too broad or too specific claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that are too broad may encompass prior art and be unpatentable. Claims that are too specific may unduly narrow protection and miss variations of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use examples (slides showing 'too broad' and 'overly specific') to find the balance; iterative review and revision is necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim drafting DOs (practical checklist)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do: Consider drafting your specification first and then your claims based on terms used in the specification. Think about what legal protection you want and tailor claims accordingly. Look at the claims in patents issued in your field. Particularly point out and distinctly claim the subject matter regarded as the invention. Review and reconcile both the specification and claims, making necessary additions and corrections so that the claim terms find support (antecedence). Check for antecedent basis issues within the claims. Ensure that dependent claims further limit the claim from which they depend. (35 USC 112(d), MPEP 608.01(n))
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow this checklist during drafting and pre-filing review; cross-check spec and claims for support and consistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim drafting CAUTIONS (do nots and pitfalls)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use claims covering multiple statutory classes of invention ('A widget and method for using same...'). Do not use non-standard transitional phrases, which may raise questions of interpretation. (MPEP 2111.03). Do not use terms inconsistently between the claims and/or specification (e.g., visor, visor member, visor section...). Do not refer back to only a portion of another claim in a dependent claim (e.g., 'The widget of the apparatus of claim 1...'). Do not use a dependent claim to remove/replace an element from a previously presented claim from which it depends. Do not use functional language that is unconnected to the structure or steps that perform the function. Do not use terms in the claim that are unsupported by the specification. Do not use trademarks or tradenames in the claims; instead use generic terms (e.g., 'hook and loop fastener' instead of Velcro®). Do not use language that merely suggests, makes optional and, thus, does not limit the claim. Avoid using negative limitations unless clearly supported by the written disclosure (specification and drawings).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat this list as drafting red flags to avoid rejections, indefiniteness, inconsistent claim interpretation, or loss of claim scope during prosecution.
